title: Enzymatic glycosylation and amidation reshapes polyene bioactivity.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and opened all three Excel supplements from Springer's static server (MOESM4 164 KB, MOESM5 85 KB, MOESM7 87 KB; all HTTP 200). MOESM7 is the Source Data workbook: 16 sheets of raw optical-density dose-response readings, horse-blood haemolysis curves, three cytotoxicity curves, a 30-mouse colony-forming-unit sheet and an 81-row pharmacokinetics sheet. Its 'Table 1' sheet holds the raw absorbance blocks behind the paper's only bioactivity table: 8 compounds x 10 fungal strains. MOESM4 is a single sheet of 84 enzyme amino-acid sequences with no activity column. I grepped the full open-access text: zero occurrences of SMILES, InChI, PubChem or ChEMBL.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The fitted half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) values themselves, which appear only as a typeset table in the article (Table 1, units micrograms per millilitre), not as a column in any downloaded file. Also taken from the text: the claim that 19 thymidine-diphosphate sugars were tested against the glycosyltransferase enzymes, and the mouse infection-model results.

a1_downloadable.note: All supplementary and source-data files download freely with no login (verified: three Excel files fetched, HTTP 200, opened successfully). Licence is Creative Commons on the article.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: Checked in the files: the potency label (IC50) is NOT a column anywhere. The Source Data workbook contains only raw plate absorbance readings laid out in positional blocks per fungal strain; each IC50 would have to be refitted with a dose-response curve, or hand-copied out of the article's typeset Table 1.

a3_inputs_present.note: Checked in the files and the full text: there is no machine-readable chemical structure anywhere. Zero SMILES, zero InChI, zero PubChem or ChEMBL identifiers. Compounds exist only as names (Nys31-Nys34, AmB-L-digitoxose) and as drawings in figures, so every structure would have to be drawn by hand.

a4_units_stated.note: Units are clearly stated and consistent: IC50 in micrograms per millilitre, haemolysis half-maximal effective concentration in micromolar, cytotoxicity concentrations in micrograms per millilitre. Seen in both the article table and the worksheet headers.

a5_enough_rows.note: KILLER. Counted in the files and the article table: 8 polyene compounds x 10 fungal strains = 80 cells, one marked ND, so 79 measured potency values. Supporting assays are smaller still: 4 compounds with haemolysis values, 2 compounds across 3 human cell lines, 30 mice. The checklist needs ~1,500 labelled rows, or ~400 for classification.

a6_fits_laptop.note: Three Excel files totalling 337 KB. Trivially fits; this is the one thing the dataset has going for it.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: The Source Data 'Table 1' sheet contains absorbance blocks for exactly the 8 compounds and 10 strains the article's Table 1 reports, and the Extended Data Fig. 1b sheet matches the triplicate conversion percentages described. No discrepancy found.

a8_label_provenance.note: Labels are genuine physical measurements, not another model's output: broth microdilution following EUCAST protocols, read as optical density at 600 nm and fitted to dose-response curves in GraphPad Prism. The raw absorbance readings are in the workbook, so provenance is fully traceable.

existing_models.name: Random-forest / support-vector-machine / LightGBM classifiers and regressors on ECFP4 chemical fingerprints for Candida albicans antifungal activity (Lagree et al. style screen, PMC12320878, 2025)
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported from search snippet only: regression models used to prioritise compounds predicted active below 10 micromolar within an applicability domain; I did not retrieve the paper's split or metric.

existing_models.name: Random forest on MHFP6 fingerprints for antimicrobial class specificity (J. Chem. Inf. Model. 2025, PMC11898080)
existing_models.score_and_split: Search snippet reports 75.9% accuracy and Cohen's kappa 0.68 for predicting which antimicrobial class a small molecule belongs to; split not retrieved.

existing_models.name: Extra Trees quantitative structure-activity regression on ~1,000 curated antifungal compounds with Morgan/ECFP4 fingerprints (Mol. Divers. 2026)
existing_models.score_and_split: Search snippet reports test R-squared 0.70 and root-mean-square error 0.38 after benchmarking 42 regression algorithms; split described only as a test set.

backbone.name: ChemBERTa or MolFormer (chemical language models that read SMILES strings)
backbone.hardware: Would run on a laptop CPU, but there is nothing to fit: 8 unique molecules and no SMILES in the files.
backbone.licence: ChemBERTa is permissively licensed (Apache/MIT via HuggingFace), so licence is not the obstacle here.

integration.partner_dataset: ChEMBL and the Community for Open Antimicrobial Drug Discovery (CO-AD D) screening set, joinable on InChIKey, plus the Fungal Genome Initiative strain records.
integration.join_key: InChIKey would be the key, but the paper supplies none, so it would first have to be generated by hand-drawing ~20 structures.
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Could not write a question that 8 compounds add anything to: pooling these few polyenes into ChEMBL's antifungal bioactivity tables would change no model's training set in a measurable way.

controls.positive_control: Available in principle: amphotericin B and nystatin A1 are the textbook reference polyenes and both were assayed against all 10 strains, so any model must rank them correctly.
controls.negative_control: Label shuffling is possible but meaningless at n=79 with 8 unique molecules; variance would swamp any signal.
controls.external_validation: Public antifungal minimum-inhibitory-concentration data for polyenes exists in ChEMBL and CO-ADD, so an external set exists, but there is no model here worth validating.

honest_claim_h3: With this data alone the only honest claim would be 'eight closely related polyene macrolides, differing at two positions, show these potencies against ten fungal strains' - a description of a small structure-activity series, not a model that predicts anything about an unseen molecule.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use the chemical structure of a polyene antifungal to predict its potency against fungi and its toxicity to blood cells.
plain_idea.train_on: Each example would be one polyene molecule paired with one fungal strain. Verified count: 8 molecules x 10 strains = 79 measured values, plus 4 molecules with red-blood-cell toxicity values.
plain_idea.predict: The half-maximal inhibitory concentration in micrograms per millilitre, measured by broth microdilution following the European Committee on Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing protocol and read as optical density at 600 nm after 48 hours.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Medicinal chemists making safer amphotericin B analogues would want to know which sugar and which amide to add before synthesising it; but 8 molecules cannot answer that, so what is actually learned here is biology from the lab work, not from a model.

more_or_better_data.why: Our 8 molecules against 10 strains is minuscule next to the ~1,000-compound curated antifungal set the 2026 Extra Trees quantitative structure-activity study used, and tiny next to ChEMBL. The only thing special is that these are new polyene derivatives, which is 8 rows.

confidence_score.why: Biological triplicates exist for each dose point, so assay noise is estimable, but with 8 unique molecules there is no way to estimate how confident a model should be about a molecule it has not seen.

models_beatable.why: The existing antifungal activity models are classical fingerprint-plus-random-forest pipelines from 2025-2026 with unclear splits, so they are beatable in principle - but not with 8 training molecules.

guaranteed_improvement.why: Fails on every condition: we cannot run their model as a baseline (weights not confirmed open), our data does not contain theirs, the assays differ (optical-density IC50 here versus mixed minimum-inhibitory-concentration sources there), and there is no shared split.

label_elsewhere.sources: ChEMBL (bioactivity database) and the Community for Open Antimicrobial Drug Discovery open screening data both hold antifungal potency for large compound sets; known resources, not searched row-by-row for this evaluation.
label_elsewhere.join_key: InChIKey or ChEMBL identifier - neither of which appears anywhere in this paper's files.
label_elsewhere.why: Antifungal potency is well measured elsewhere, which is exactly why this paper's 79 values add nothing: the training data and the external validation set would both have to come from somewhere else entirely.

ml_idea: The project considered was predicting antifungal potency and red-blood-cell toxicity of modified polyene macrolides from chemical structure, so that chemists could choose which sugar and amide modification to make before running a synthesis. It dies on sample size: the paper reports 79 potency values across 8 molecules. A salvageable variant - predicting which bacterial glycosyltransferase enzyme accepts which sugar donor, from the enzyme sequence - also fails, because the 84 enzyme sequences in the supplement carry no activity labels and the conversion measurements cover only 4 enzymes against 2 acceptors.

effort.compute_note: Estimated, not timed beyond opening the three workbooks (each parsed in under a second). The 6 hours is hand-drawing ~20 polyene structures into SMILES and refitting dose-response curves from the raw absorbance blocks; the modelling itself would take seconds because there is almost no data.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count the potency values: open the article's Table 1 or the 'Table 1' sheet of the Source Data workbook and count compounds times strains. It is 8 x 10 = 80, one of them not determined. That single count kills the project in two minutes, and it is the check I did.

verdict_reason: Fails Part A on three counts, the decisive one being A5 sample size: 79 measured potency values across just 8 polyene molecules, verified by opening the Source Data workbook, against a threshold of ~1,500 rows. It also fails A3 (no SMILES, InChI or any machine-readable structure anywhere in the files or text, so inputs would be hand-drawn) and A2 (the IC50 label is not a column - the supplement contains only raw plate absorbance readings in positional blocks, and the fitted values appear only in the article's typeset table). This is an excellent piece of enzymology and a genuinely promising drug lead, but it is a focused structure-activity series, not a dataset.
